question: how attention works in a transformer

definition.title: How attention works in a transformer
definition.summary: Each token scores every token with a query-key dot product, turns the scores into weights, and blends their values; based on general knowledge, as no source text was supplied.

beats.caption: Alone, the vector for "it" carries no information about which earlier word it refers to.
beats.explanation: A transformer represents every token as a vector. Attention is the step that lets each token's vector be rewritten using information from the rest of the sequence.

beats.caption: Attention gives "it" one weight per token, summing to 1, and here most of the weight lands on "cat".
beats.explanation: These numbers are invented for illustration. Every token gets its own row of weights like this one, so the full result is a table of weights between all pairs of tokens.

beats.caption: The token being updated emits a query vector, a learned description of what it is looking for.
beats.explanation: This is a simplified two-dimensional picture with made-up coordinates. Real query vectors have dozens to hundreds of dimensions.

beats.caption: Every token in the sequence offers a key vector, a learned description of what it contains.
beats.explanation: Only three of the seven keys are drawn to keep the picture readable. Queries and keys live in the same space so that they can be compared directly.

beats.caption: The score is the dot product of query and key: 3.5 for the well-aligned "cat" key, 0 for the perpendicular "as" key.
beats.explanation: A dot product grows when two vectors point the same way, so alignment means relevance; the "hid" key scores 1.6. Real transformers also divide the scores by the square root of the key dimension, which is omitted here.

scenes.title: From scores to a new vector

beats.caption: Dot products with all seven keys give "it" one raw score per token.
beats.explanation: The scores for "cat", "hid" and "as" are the ones from the previous picture; the others are invented in the same way. Raw scores can be any size, so they are not yet usable as proportions.

beats.caption: Softmax exponentiates and normalises the scores into positive weights that sum to 1, sharpening the lead of "cat".
beats.explanation: Each weight is e raised to the score, divided by the total over all tokens. Because of the exponential, a modest gap in score becomes a large gap in weight.

beats.caption: Each token also offers a value vector, and the new vector for "it" is the sum of those values weighted by attention.
beats.explanation: Here 63% of the mix comes from the value of "cat", so the updated vector now carries information about its referent. The key decides whether a token is attended to; the value decides what it contributes.

scenes.title: One attention head, end to end

nodes.label: query
nodes.detail: The vector of the token being updated, multiplied by the learned matrix W_Q. It encodes what this token is looking for.

nodes.label: keys
nodes.detail: Each token's vector multiplied by the learned matrix W_K. A key encodes what the token can be matched on.

nodes.label: values
nodes.detail: Each token's vector multiplied by the learned matrix W_V. A value is the content the token passes on if it is attended to.

beats.caption: Three learned matrices turn token vectors into queries, keys and values, and everything after that is fixed arithmetic.
beats.explanation: Every token runs this as the query at the same time. A transformer runs several such heads side by side, each with its own matrices, and stacks many layers of them.

takeaways: Attention rewrites each token's vector as a weighted mix of value vectors from the whole sequence.
The weights are a softmax over query-key dot products, so what counts as relevant is learned rather than hard-coded.
Multiple heads and stacked layers repeat this step, each able to capture a different kind of relationship.
